extraction_notes.note: There are no theorem environments; the results are simulation findings read off figures. Each finding the text states is a claim with rigor numerical; figure captions (which repeat or add numbers) are not nodes.
The optimization problems are numbered equations; per the rules the equations stay equation nodes, and each is nested in a prose problem node spanning the sentence that introduces it.

Appendix A applies the read-error convolution to the count vector z rather than to the frequencies z/r, reuses $M'$ (earlier M+D) for the augmented matrix, and never defines z'; with the 1/2 prefactor the -1 column contributes $-x_{N+1}/2$, not $-x_{N+1}$.
R and L are used in the Gamma coverage assumption before they are defined in the 'Targeted region length' paragraph; the edge DP22->AssumP2 is backward.

DP4 is introduced as an example of a UUP matrix but defines the term used later, so definition; ClP2 (Eq. 8) could be a model definition of q, kept as a claim since the text says it is 'therefore obtained' from the read-error assumption.

The abstract's headline (4 carriers among over 4000 individuals with about 10 lanes and 10 barcodes) is stated nowhere in the body, so it is not a node; the introduction's account of prior designs (Prabhu & Pe'er, Erlich et al.) and the discussion's future directions (adaptive pooling, LD, CNVs) are prose without stated results.
The pooled-sequencing protocol, the informal statement of the identification goal and the simulation protocol are prose procedures; their spans and step splits are judgment.

sec:rare_cs_framework.section: Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Compressed sensing measurements
nodes.statement: In a standard {\bf CS } problem one wishes to reconstruct a sparse vector $\textbf{x}$ of length $N$, by taking $k$ different measurements $y_i = \textbf{m}_{i} \cdot \textbf{x}, \: i=1,\ldots,k$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard CS: recover a sparse length-$N$ vector x from $k$ linear measurements $y_i=\mathbf{m}_i\cdot\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Measurement (sensing) matrix
nodes.statement: This may be represented as solving the following set of linear equations \begin{equation} M \bf{x} = \textbf{y} \end{equation} where $M$ is a $k \times N$ {\it measurement matrix} or {\it sensing matrix}, whose rows are the different $\textbf{m}_i$'s (as a general rule, we use upper-case letters to denote matrices: $M,E,..$, lower boldface letters to denote vectors: $\textbf{x}, \textbf{y}, ..$ and lower case to denote scalars: $x,y,x_i$.)
nodes.statement_short: The measurements form the linear system $M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$ with $M$ the $k\times N$ sensing matrix; notation conventions.

nodes.name: Linear measurement system $M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$
nodes.statement: M \bf{x} = \textbf{y}
nodes.label: eq:cs_classic

nodes.name: Compressed sensing unique recovery
nodes.statement: However, it has been shown that if $\textbf{x}$ is sparse, and $M$ has certain properties, the original vector $\textbf{x}$ can be recovered uniquely from Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_classic}) \cite{Candes:01,Donoho:01}. More specifically, a unique solution is found in case $k > C s \log (N/s)$, where $C$ is a constant, and $s$ is the is the number of non-zero entries in $\textbf{x}$.
assumptions: $C$ is a constant, and $s$ is the is the number of non-zero entries in $\textbf{x}$
conclusions: the original vector $\textbf{x}$ can be recovered uniquely from Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_classic})
nodes.statement_short: A sparse x is uniquely recoverable from $k > C s\log(N/s)$ measurements by a suitable $M$.

nodes.name: Uniform Uncertainty Principle (Restricted Isometry Property)
nodes.statement: A sensing matrix which allows for a correct reconstruction of $\textbf{x}$ posses a property known as ``Uniform Uncertainty Principle'' (UUP) or Restricted Isometry Property (RIP)~\cite{candes2005decoding,candes2005stable}. Briefly, UUP states that any subset of the columns of $M$ of size $2s$ form a matrix which is almost orthogonal (although since $k<N$ the columns cannot be perfectly orthogonal), which, in practice, makes the matrix $M$ ``invertible'' for sparse vectors $\textbf{x}$.
differentia: any subset of the columns of $M$ of size $2s$ form a matrix which is almost orthogonal
nodes.statement_short: UUP/RIP: every $2s$ columns of $M$ are nearly orthogonal, making $M$ invertible on sparse vectors.

nodes.name: Bernoulli matrix
nodes.statement: As an example of a UUP matrix consider a Bernoulli matrix, namely a matrix whose entries are independent random variables set to be $1$ or $-1$ with probability $0.5$\footnote{It is common to require orthonormality of the columns therefore the entries should also be divided by $\sqrt{k}$.}.
differentia: entries are independent random variables set to be $1$ or $-1$ with probability $0.5$

nodes.name: Random Bernoulli matrices satisfy UUP
nodes.statement: It is known that almost any instance of such a random matrix will satisfy UUP with an overwhelming probability~\cite{donoho2006most,candes2006near} (the same is true when each entry in the matrix is a standard Gaussian random variable.)
conclusions: almost any instance of such a random matrix will satisfy UUP with an overwhelming probability
nodes.statement_short: Random Bernoulli (or Gaussian) matrices satisfy UUP with overwhelming probability.

nodes.name: $\ell_0$ sparse recovery problem
nodes.statement: Once $M$ and $\textbf{y}$ are given, {\bf CS } aims to find the sparsest possible $\textbf{x}$ which obeys Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_classic}). This can be written as the following optimization problem: \begin{equation} {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_0 \quad s.t. \: \: M \textbf{x}=\textbf{y} \end{equation} where the $\ell_0$ norm $||\textbf{x}||_0 \equiv \sum_{i} 1_{\{x_i \neq 0\}}$ simply counts the number of non-zero elements in $\textbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find the sparsest x (minimum $\ell_0$ norm) with $M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}$.

nodes.name: $\ell_0$ minimization
nodes.statement: {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_0 \quad s.t. \: \: M \textbf{x}=\textbf{y}
nodes.label: eq:cs_problem

nodes.name: Intractability of $\ell_0$ minimization
nodes.statement: Problem (\ref{eq:cs_problem}) involves a non-convex $\ell_0$ term and can be shown to be computationally intractable in general \cite{candes2005error}.
conclusions: can be shown to be computationally intractable in general

nodes.name: $\ell_1$ relaxation equivalence
nodes.statement: However, another impressive breakthrough of {\bf CS } theory is that one can relax this constraint to the closest convex $\ell_p$ norm, namely the $\ell_1$ norm, and still get a solution which, under certain conditions, is identical to the solution of problem (\ref{eq:cs_problem}).
conclusions: one can relax this constraint to the closest convex $\ell_p$ norm, namely the $\ell_1$ norm, and still get a solution which, under certain conditions, is identical to the solution of problem (\ref{eq:cs_problem})
nodes.statement_short: Under conditions, the convex $\ell_1$ relaxation has the same solution as the $\ell_0$ problem.

nodes.name: $\ell_1$ minimization (basis pursuit)
nodes.statement: Hence the problem is reformulated as the following $\ell_1$ minimization problem, which can be efficiently solved by convex optimization techniques: \begin{equation} {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: M \textbf{x}=\textbf{y} \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\ell_1$ minimization
nodes.statement: {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: M \textbf{x}=\textbf{y}
nodes.label: eq:cs_problem_L1

nodes.name: Noisy $\ell_1$ minimization
nodes.statement: In most realistic {\bf CS } problems measurements are corrupted by noise, hence Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_classic}) is replaced by $M \textbf{x} + \bm{\eta} = \textbf{y}$, where $\bm{\eta}=(\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{k})$ are the unknown errors in each of the $k$ measurements, and the total measurement noise, given by the $\ell_2$ norm of $\bm{\eta}$ is assumed to be small. Therefore, the optimization problem is reformulated as follows: \begin{equation} {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: ||M \textbf{x} - \textbf{y}||_2 \leq \epsilon \end{equation} where $\epsilon > 0$ is set to be the maximal level of noise we are able to tolerate, while still obtaining a sparse solution.
nodes.statement_short: With noisy measurements $M\mathbf{x}+\eta=\mathbf{y}$, minimize $\|x\|_1$ s.t. $\|Mx-y\|_2\le\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Noisy $\ell_1$ minimization
nodes.statement: {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: ||M \textbf{x} - \textbf{y}||_2 \leq \epsilon
nodes.label: eq:cs_problemFinal

nodes.name: Robustness of CS reconstruction to noise
nodes.statement: It is known that {\bf CS } reconstruction is robust to noise, thus adding the noise term $\epsilon$ does not cause a breakdown of the {\bf CS } machinery, but merely leads to a possible increase in the number of measurements $k$ \cite{candes2005stable}.
conclusions: {\bf CS } reconstruction is robust to noise
does not cause a breakdown of the {\bf CS } machinery, but merely leads to a possible increase in the number of measurements $k$

nodes.name: Number of individuals $N$
nodes.statement: We wish to reconstruct the genotypes of $N$ individuals at a specific locus.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Genotype vector
nodes.statement: The genotypes are represented by a vector $\textbf{x}$ of length $N$, where $x_i$ represents the genotype of the {\it i}'th individual.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Reference and alternative alleles $A$, $B$
nodes.statement: We denote the reference allele by $A$, and the alternative allele by $B$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Genotype encoding $x_i\in\{0,1,2\}$
nodes.statement: The possible entries of $x_{i}$ are $0$, $1$ and $2$, representing a homozygous reference allele ($AA$), a heterozygous allele ($AB$) and a homozygous alternative allele ($BB$), respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
nodes.statement_short: $x_i\in\{0,1,2\}$ encodes genotypes AA, AB, BB (number of B alleles).

nodes.name: Integer genotypes ease reconstruction
nodes.statement: In classic {\bf CS } the unknown variables are typically real numbers. The restriction on $\textbf{x}$ in this case is expected to reduce the number of measurements needed for reconstruction and may also enable using faster reconstruction algorithms, as it is known that even a weaker restriction, namely that all entries are positive, already simplifies the reconstruction problem \cite{Donoho:positive}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
nodes.statement_short: The integer restriction on x is expected to reduce the measurements needed; even positivity already helps (Donoho).

nodes.name: Bernoulli(0.5) pooling design
nodes.statement: The sensing matrix $M$ is built of $k$ different measurements represented by the rows of $M$. The entry $m_{ij}$ is set to $1$ if the {\it j}'th individual participates in {\it i}'th measurement, and zero otherwise. Each measurement includes a random subset of individuals, where the probability to include a certain individual is $0.5$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
differentia: The entry $m_{ij}$ is set to $1$ if the {\it j}'th individual participates in {\it i}'th measurement, and zero otherwise
the probability to include a certain individual is $0.5$
nodes.statement_short: Pool $i$ contains each individual independently with probability 0.5; $m_{ij}=1$ iff individual $j$ is in pool $i$.

nodes.name: Pooling matrix is a good sensing matrix
nodes.statement: Hence, $M$ is equivalent to the Bernoulli matrix mentioned in Section~\ref{sec:csIntro}, which is known to be a ``good'' sensing matrix\footnote{This is easily seen by using the simple linear transformation $x \to (2x-1)/\sqrt{k}$.} (another type of a sensing matrix, in which only $\sim\!\! \sqrt{N}$ elements in each measurement are non-zero is considered in Section~\ref{sec:Results}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
conclusions: $M$ is equivalent to the Bernoulli matrix mentioned in Section~\ref{sec:csIntro}, which is known to be a ``good'' sensing matrix
nodes.statement_short: The 0/1 pooling matrix is an affine transform of a $\pm1$ Bernoulli matrix, hence a good sensing matrix.

nodes.name: Pooled sequencing measurement protocol
nodes.statement: In practice, measurements are performed by taking equal amounts of DNA from the individuals chosen to participate in the specific pool, thus their contribution to the mixture is approximately equal. Then, the mixture is amplified using PCR, which ensures that the amplification bias generated by the PCR process affects all individuals equally \cite{Ingman:01}. Finally, DNA of each pool is sequenced in a separate lane, and reads are mapped back to the reference genome (this may be performed using standard alignment algorithms such as MAQ \cite{li2008mapping}.)
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
nodes.statement_short: Mix equal DNA amounts per pool, PCR-amplify, sequence each pool in its own lane and map reads to the reference.

nodes.name: Mix equal DNA amounts
nodes.statement: In practice, measurements are performed by taking equal amounts of DNA from the individuals chosen to participate in the specific pool, thus their contribution to the mixture is approximately equal.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: PCR amplification
nodes.statement: Then, the mixture is amplified using PCR, which ensures that the amplification bias generated by the PCR process affects all individuals equally \cite{Ingman:01}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Sequence each pool and map reads
nodes.statement: Finally, DNA of each pool is sequenced in a separate lane, and reads are mapped back to the reference genome (this may be performed using standard alignment algorithms such as MAQ \cite{li2008mapping}.)
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Reads per pool $r$
nodes.statement: For each locus of interest we record the number of reads containing the rare allele together with the {\it total} number of reads covering this locus in each pool, denoted by $r$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Measurement vector $\mathbf{y}$ (pool frequencies)
nodes.statement: These numbers provide the measurement vector $\textbf{y}$ representing the $k$ frequencies obtained for this locus in the $k$ different pools.
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework

nodes.name: Rare-allele carrier identification
nodes.statement: For each locus, our goal is to reconstruct the vector $\textbf{x}$, given the sensing matrix $M$ and the measurement vector $\textbf{y}$, while realizing that some measurement error $\epsilon$ is present (see Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_problemFinal}).)
nodes.section: 2.2 Rare-Allele Identification in a {\bf CS } Framework
nodes.statement_short: Per locus, reconstruct the genotype vector x from the pooling matrix M and noisy pool frequencies y.

nodes.name: Rare-allele frequency $f$
nodes.statement: The fraction of individuals with the rare allele is denoted $f$, thus the vector $\textbf{x}$ has $s = f N$ non-zero elements\footnote{Here and throughout the paper we define the fraction of {\it individuals} (rather than alleles) as the `rare-allele-frequency' - thus the fraction of alternative {\it alleles}, assuming Hardy-Weinberg (HW) equilibrium, is in fact $1-\sqrt{1-f}$.}.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ = fraction of carrier individuals, so x has $s=fN$ non-zeros (allele frequency is $1-\sqrt{1-f}$ under HW).

nodes.name: Normalized pooling matrix $\hat M$
nodes.statement: $M$ is a $k \times N$ Bernoulli sensing matrix, and denote by $\hat{M}$ the normalized version of $M$ whose entries represent the fraction of each individual's DNA in each pool: \begin{equation} \hat{m}_{ij} \equiv \frac{m_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} m_{ij}} \end{equation}
differentia: entries represent the fraction of each individual's DNA in each pool

nodes.name: Row normalization $\hat m_{ij}$
nodes.statement: \hat{m}_{ij} \equiv \frac{m_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} m_{ij}}

nodes.name: Perfect unbiased mixing
nodes.statement: Assume that the mixing of DNA is perfect and unbiased, and that each DNA segment from each individual in a pool is equally likely to be read by the sequencing machinery.

nodes.name: B-allele read probability $q_i$
nodes.statement: Suppose that a read from the {\it i}'th pool is drawn from a DNA segment covering our desired locus. It is then expected that this read will contain the $B$ allele with probability $q_i \equiv \frac{1}{2}\hat{\textbf{m}}_i \cdot \textbf{x}$, where $\hat{\textbf{m}}_i$ is the {\it i}'th row of $\hat{M}$ (the $\frac{1}{2}$ pre-factor is due to the fact that both alleles are sequenced for each individual.)
nodes.statement_short: A read from pool $i$ carries allele B with probability $q_i=\frac12\hat{\mathbf m}_i\cdot\mathbf x$.

nodes.name: Pool B-allele frequency vector $\mathbf q$
nodes.statement: The vector of frequencies of the $B$ allele, for each of the $k$ pools is therefore: \begin{equation} \textbf{q}=\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x} \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\mathbf q=\frac12\hat M\mathbf x$
nodes.statement: \textbf{q}=\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}

nodes.name: Binomial read sampling
nodes.statement: In practice a specific position is covered by a limited number of reads, which we denote by $r$, and the number of reads from the rare alleles $\textbf{z}$ out of the total number of reads $r$ is binomially distributed $z_{i}\sim Binomial(r,q_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: The rare-allele read counts $z_i$ out of $r$ reads are Binomial$(r,q_i)$.

nodes.name: Gamma-distributed coverage
nodes.statement: The distribution of $r$ over different loci depends on the experimental conditions, and was shown to follow a Gamma distribution in certain cases \cite{Prabhu:01}. We adopt this assumption, draw $r$ for each locus from a Gamma distribution $r \sim \Gamma(\frac{R}{L}, 1)$, and apply it to all $k$ pools.
nodes.statement_short: Per-locus read count $r\sim\Gamma(R/L,1)$ (following Prabhu & Pe'er), shared by all pools.

nodes.name: Sampling noise
nodes.statement: This binomial sampling process provides measurements which are close, yet not identical to the expected frequency of the rare allele $r q_i$, and these fluctuations are regarded as {\it sampling noise}.

nodes.name: Integer CS problem with sampling noise
nodes.statement: Therefore the {\bf CS } problem formulation is given by (compare to Eq.~(\ref{eq:cs_problemFinal})): \begin{eqnarray} \textbf{x}^* = \underset{\textbf{x} \in \{0,1,2\}^N}{argmin} \|\textbf{x}\|_{1} \quad {\mbox s.t.} \: \: ||\frac{1}{2} \hat{M}\textbf{x}-\frac{1}{r}\textbf{z}||_2 < \epsilon \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\|x\|_1$ over $x\in\{0,1,2\}^N$ s.t. $\|\frac12\hat Mx - z/r\|_2<\epsilon$.

nodes.name: CS problem with sampling noise
nodes.statement: \textbf{x}^* = \underset{\textbf{x} \in \{0,1,2\}^N}{argmin} \|\textbf{x}\|_{1} \quad {\mbox s.t.} \: \: ||\frac{1}{2} \hat{M}\textbf{x}-\frac{1}{r}\textbf{z}||_2 < \epsilon
nodes.label: eq:CSopt

nodes.name: Read error $e_r$
nodes.statement: All of these can be modeled using a single parameter $e_r$, which represents the probability that the base read is different from the base of the measured sample's DNA at a given locus.

nodes.name: Errors always produce allele B
nodes.statement: The resulting base can be any of the other three different nucleotides, however we conservatively assume that the errors will {\it always} produce the alternative allele $B$ (if, for example the reference allele is `G' and the alternative allele is `T', we assume that all erroneous reads produce `T'. In practice, some reads will produce `A' and `C', and these can be immediately discarded thus reducing the effective error rate.)

nodes.name: B-read probability under read error
nodes.statement: The probability of observing $B$ at a certain read is therefore obtained by a convolution of the frequency of $B$ alleles and the read error: \begin{equation} \textbf{q} = (1-e_r) \frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x} + e_r (1-\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}) \end{equation}
conclusions: \textbf{q} = (1-e_r) \frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x} + e_r (1-\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x})
nodes.statement_short: With read error, B is observed with probability $(1-e_r)q+e_r(1-q)$.

nodes.name: Read-error convolution of $\mathbf q$
nodes.statement: \textbf{q} = (1-e_r) \frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x} + e_r (1-\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x})
nodes.label: eq:q_vec

nodes.name: Known, lane-independent read error
nodes.statement: We assume that $e_r$ is known to the researcher, and that it is similar across different lanes.

nodes.name: Read-error-corrected CS problem
nodes.statement: In this case, one can correct for the convolution in Eq.~(\ref{eq:q_vec}) and obtain the following problem: \begin{eqnarray} \textbf{x}^* = \underset{\textbf{x} \in \{0,1,2\}^N}{argmin} \|\textbf{x}\|_{1} \quad {\mbox s.t.} \: \: ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}-( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)||_2 < \epsilon \end{eqnarray} Hence the measurement vector in our problem equals $\textbf{y} = ( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)$ and the sensing matrix is $\frac{1}{2} \hat{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Invert the read-error convolution: measurements $y=(z/r-e_r)/(1-2e_r)$, sensing matrix $\frac12\hat M$, integer $\ell_1$ minimization.

nodes.name: Read-error-corrected CS problem
nodes.statement: \textbf{x}^* = \underset{\textbf{x} \in \{0,1,2\}^N}{argmin} \|\textbf{x}\|_{1} \quad {\mbox s.t.} \: \: ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}-( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)||_2 < \epsilon
nodes.label: eq:CSopt_noise

nodes.name: Estimating an unknown read error
nodes.statement: If $e_r$ is unknown, one may still estimate it, for example by running one lane with a single region on a single individual with known genotypes. Alternatively, we show in Appendix \ref{app:unknown_p_err} how to incorporate the estimation of the read error term $e_r$ within our {\bf CS } framework from the overlapping pooled sequence data.
nodes.statement_short: An unknown $e_r$ can be estimated from a control lane, or learned within the CS problem (Appendix A).

nodes.name: DNA preparation (DP) errors
nodes.statement: Finally we add to our model one more source of noise, namely DNA preparation errors ({DP } errors.)

nodes.name: Actual measurement matrix $M'$
nodes.statement: While $M$ is our original zero-one Bernoulli matrix, the actual measurement matrix $M'$ is obtained by adding {DP } errors to each non-zero entry.

nodes.name: DP error matrix $D$
nodes.statement: Hence, the true mixture matrix is $M' \equiv M+D$, where the {DP } matrix $D$ adds a centered Gaussian random variable to each non-zero entry of $M$: \begin{eqnarray} d_{ij} \sim \left\{\begin{array}{ll} N(0,\sigma^2) \hspace{1cm} \mbox{if} \:\: m_{ij}=1 \\ \equiv 0 \hspace{1.6cm} otherwise. \end{array} \right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $M'=M+D$, where $D$ adds $N(0,\sigma^2)$ noise to each non-zero entry of $M$.

nodes.name: DP error distribution $d_{ij}$
nodes.statement: d_{ij} \sim \left\{\begin{array}{ll} N(0,\sigma^2) \hspace{1cm} \mbox{if} \:\: m_{ij}=1 \\ \equiv 0 \hspace{1.6cm} otherwise. \end{array} \right.

nodes.name: DP errors perturb the sensing matrix
nodes.statement: The matrix $M'$ is unknown and we only have access to $M$, hence the form of Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}) in this case is unchanged. $M'$ takes effect indirectly by modifying $\textbf{q}$, which effects $\textbf{z}$ the actual number of reads from the rare allele. As opposed to a classic {\bf CS } problem in which the sensing matrix is usually assumed to be known exactly, {DP } effectively introduces noise into the matrix itself. We study this effect of {DP } errors in Section~\ref{sec:Results}, and show that a standard {\bf CS } approach is robust to such noise.
nodes.statement_short: $M'$ is unknown, so the problem is unchanged; DP errors act as noise in the sensing matrix itself.

nodes.name: Expected reads per locus $E[r]=R/L$
nodes.statement: The expected number of reads from a certain locus is determined by the total number of reads in a lane $R$ and the number of loci covered in a single lane $L$, and is given by $E[r] = \frac{R}{L}$ (the actual number of reads from each locus $r$ follows a Gamma distribution with mean $\frac{R}{L}$.)

nodes.name: Aligned reads per lane $R$
nodes.statement: $R$ is defined as the number of reads which were successfully aligned to our regions of interest.

nodes.name: Fixed lane throughput $R=4\cdot10^6$
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper we have fixed $R$ to be $R = 4000000$, representing a rather conservative estimate of a modern Illumina genome analyzer's run (e.g. compare to~\cite{mardis2008impact}), and also assuming that targeted selection efficiency is very high (it is reported to be $\sim90\!\%$ in \cite{gnirke2009solution}.)

nodes.name: Average coverage per individual per SNP $c$
nodes.statement: Another important and related parameter is the {\it average coverage per individual per SNP}, denoted $c$, which is given by: \begin{equation} c = \frac{R/L}{N/2} \Big({\equiv \frac{E[r]}{N/2}}\Big) \end{equation}
definiendum: average coverage per individual per SNP

nodes.name: Coverage $c$
nodes.statement: c = \frac{R/L}{N/2} \Big({\equiv \frac{E[r]}{N/2}}\Big)
nodes.label: eq:coverage

nodes.name: Per-individual coverage is approximately $c$
nodes.statement: When the total number of reads in a pool $r$ is given, the actual coverage obtained for each person in a pool has a distribution which is approximately $Binomial(r, 1/N_{pooled})$, where $N_{pooled} \sim \frac{N}{2}$ is the number of individuals in the pool. Therefore the average coverage per individual in a given pool is indeed approximately $c$.
assumptions: the total number of reads in a pool $r$ is given
$N_{pooled} \sim \frac{N}{2}$ is the number of individuals in the pool
conclusions: the actual coverage obtained for each person in a pool has a distribution which is approximately $Binomial(r, 1/N_{pooled})$
the average coverage per individual in a given pool is indeed approximately $c$

nodes.name: Measured pool frequencies, N=3000, f=0.1%
nodes.statement: In order to visualize the effect of the three noise factors, i.e., sampling noise, read errors and {DP } errors, Fig.~\ref{fig:actualValues} presents the measured values $\textbf{y}$ in a specific scenario. We simulate an instance of $N=3000$ individuals and rare allele frequency $f=0.1\%$, tested over $k=100$ lanes. Hence we have three heterozygotic carriers to be identified, and, in the absence of noise, the measurement in each lane should display four levels, which correspond to whether $0$, $1$, $2$ or $3$ of the carriers are actually present in the specific pool. In order to display the effect of sampling noise, we consider three values for the average coverage $c$ , i.e., number of reads per individual per SNP: $27$, $267$ and an infinite number of reads, which corresponds to zero sampling noise. Each of these three values appears on a separate row in Fig.~\ref{fig:actualValues}. The panels on the left hand side of Fig.~\ref{fig:actualValues} correspond to read error $e_{r}=1\%$, while on the right hand side there is no read error at all. The data in all panels contain {DP } errors with $\sigma=0.05$. Each panel also displays the actual number of reconstruction errors in each case, namely the Hamming distance between the correct vector $\textbf{x}$ and reconstructed vector $\textbf{x}^*$ obtained by solving Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}). The effect of sampling noise is clearly visible in Fig.~\ref{fig:actualValues}. An infinite amount of reads (lower row; (e),(f)), causes the measurements to be very close to their expected frequency, where slight deviations are only due to {DP } errors and the fact that the pool size is not exactly $N/2$. For a moderate number of reads ($c=267$ - middle row; (c),(d)) the measurements follow the expected frequency levels when there are no read errors (right panel (d)), but this rough quantization completely vanishes for $e_{r}=1\%$ (left panel (c).) However, reconstruction was accurate even in this case, because our {\bf CS } formulation (Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise})) takes these errors into account and aggregate the information from {\it all} lanes to enable reconstruction. When the number of reads per person is small ($c=27$ - upper row; (a),(b)), the four levels disappear irrespective of the read error. Reconstruction is still accurate in the absence of read errors (right panel (b)), and there are $4$ errors in the reconstructed genotype vector ${\textbf{x}}^*$ when $e_{r}=1\%$ (left panel (a)), which probably implies that sampling noise is too high in this case. While a coverage of $27$ reads per person is overwhelmingly sufficient when sequencing a {\it single} individual, it leads to errors in the reconstruction when pooling many individuals together.
nodes.statement_short: 3 carriers among 3000 over 100 pools: measured frequencies at coverage 27, 267, infinity with/without 1% read error; quantization lost and errors at low coverage.

nodes.name: GPSR reconstruction with integer post-processing
nodes.statement: We use the Gradient Projection for Sparse Reconstruction algorithm (GPSR)~\cite{GPSR:01}, to solve the optimization problem~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}). GPSR is designed to solve a slightly different, but equivalent, formulation as in Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}): \begin{equation} {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} \quad ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}-( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)||_2 + \tau ||\textbf{x}||_1 \end{equation} where the parameter $\tau$ provides the trade-off between the equations fit and the sparsity promoting factor, and is equivalent to specifying the maximal allowed error $\epsilon$. It is often desirable in applications to let the parameter $\tau$ scale with $||M^{\textbf{T}}{\textbf{y}}||_{\infty}$ \cite{kim2007interior}, where in our case $\textbf{y}=( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)$ corresponds to the measurements. We have chosen to adopt this scaling throughout this paper, and have set $\tau=0.01||\hat{M}^{\textbf{T}}{\textbf{y}}||_{\infty}$, although experimentation with different values of $\tau$ did not alter results significantly. GPSR outputs a sparse vector ${\textbf{x}}^*$ with a few non-zero real entries, but does not use the fact that our variables are integers from the set $\{0,1,2\}$. We therefore perform a post-processing step in order to obtain such a solution. Simple rounding of the continuous results in ${\textbf{x}}^*$ may obtain such a vector\footnote{by `rounding' here we mean reducing to the set $\{0,1,2\}$. Thus any negative number is `rounded' to zero and any number larger than $2$ is `rounded' to $2$.}. We chose a different post-processing scheme, which yields better performance: we rank all non-zero values obtained by GPSR, and round the largest $s$ non-zero values, setting to zero all other $N-s$ values to get the vector ${\textbf{x}}^{*s}$. We then compute an error term $err_s \equiv ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M} {\textbf{x}}^{*s} - \textbf{y}||_2$. Repeating this for different values of $s$ we select the vector ${\textbf{x}}^{*s}$ which minimizes the error term $err_s$. Thus the final solution's sparsity $s$ is always smaller or equal to the sparsity of the vector obtained by GPSR.
input: the sensing matrix $M$ and the measurement vector $\textbf{y}$
output: the vector ${\textbf{x}}^{*s}$ which minimizes the error term $err_s$
nodes.statement_short: Solve the penalized $\ell_1$ problem with GPSR, then round the top-$s$ entries to $\{0,1,2\}$ and pick the $s$ minimizing the residual.

nodes.name: Run GPSR
nodes.statement: We use the Gradient Projection for Sparse Reconstruction algorithm (GPSR)~\cite{GPSR:01}, to solve the optimization problem~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}).

nodes.name: GPSR penalized formulation
nodes.statement: GPSR is designed to solve a slightly different, but equivalent, formulation as in Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}): \begin{equation} {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} \quad ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}-( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)||_2 + \tau ||\textbf{x}||_1 \end{equation} where the parameter $\tau$ provides the trade-off between the equations fit and the sparsity promoting factor, and is equivalent to specifying the maximal allowed error $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Unconstrained form: minimize residual norm plus $\tau\|x\|_1$; $\tau$ plays the role of $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: GPSR objective
nodes.statement: {\textbf{x}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x}}{argmin} \quad ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M}\textbf{x}-( \frac{1}{r}\textbf{z} - e_r ) / (1-2 e_r)||_2 + \tau ||\textbf{x}||_1
nodes.label: eq:cs_problem_GPSR

nodes.name: Set the regularization $\tau$
nodes.statement: We have chosen to adopt this scaling throughout this paper, and have set $\tau=0.01||\hat{M}^{\textbf{T}}{\textbf{y}}||_{\infty}$, although experimentation with different values of $\tau$ did not alter results significantly.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\tau=0.01\|\hat M^T y\|_\infty$.

nodes.name: Round the top-$s$ values
nodes.statement: we rank all non-zero values obtained by GPSR, and round the largest $s$ non-zero values, setting to zero all other $N-s$ values to get the vector ${\textbf{x}}^{*s}$.

nodes.name: Residual of the rounded vector
nodes.statement: We then compute an error term $err_s \equiv ||\frac{1}{2}\hat{M} {\textbf{x}}^{*s} - \textbf{y}||_2$.

nodes.name: Choose $s$ minimizing the residual
nodes.statement: Repeating this for different values of $s$ we select the vector ${\textbf{x}}^{*s}$ which minimizes the error term $err_s$.

nodes.name: Barcode
nodes.statement: A barcode is obtained by attaching to the DNA in each sample a unique DNA sequence of about $5$ additional nucleotides, which enables the unique identification of this sample \cite{hamady2008error}.
nodes.genus: unique DNA sequence of about $5$ additional nucleotides
differentia: enables the unique identification of this sample

nodes.name: Pooled-barcodes design
nodes.statement: In a pooled-barcodes design \cite{Erlich:01}, the DNA in each pool (as opposed to the DNA of a specific individual) is tagged using a unique barcode.

nodes.name: Number of barcodes $n_{bar}$
nodes.statement: If $n_{bar}$ different barcodes are available, we may apply $n_{bar}$ pools to a single lane and still identify the pool from which each read originated (although not the specific individual.)

nodes.name: CS with barcoded pools
nodes.statement: We utilize barcodes by increasing the number of effective lanes while the number of reads per lane is decreased. The usage of $k$ lanes and $n_{bar}$ barcodes is simply translated into solving problem (\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}) with $k \times n_{bar}$ pools and $R/n_{bar}$ total reads per lane.
nodes.statement_short: Treat $k$ lanes with $n_{bar}$ barcodes as $k n_{bar}$ pools of $R/n_{bar}$ reads each and solve the same CS problem.

nodes.name: Simulation protocol
nodes.statement: Various parameter ranges were simulated, where each set of parameters was tested in $500$ instances. In each simulation we have generated an input genotype vector $\textbf{x}$, applied measurements according to our mathematical model, and have tried to reconstruct $\textbf{x}$ from these measurements.
nodes.statement_short: For each parameter set, 500 times: draw x, simulate pooled measurements under the noise model, reconstruct.

nodes.name: Repeat 500 instances per parameter set
nodes.statement: Various parameter ranges were simulated, where each set of parameters was tested in $500$ instances.

nodes.name: Generate, measure, reconstruct
nodes.statement: In each simulation we have generated an input genotype vector $\textbf{x}$, applied measurements according to our mathematical model, and have tried to reconstruct $\textbf{x}$ from these measurements.

nodes.name: Reconstruction error
nodes.statement: Each entry $i$ for which $x_i$ is different from $x^*_i$ is termed a reconstruction error, and implies that the genotype for a certain individual was not reconstructed correctly, yielding either a false positive ($x_i = 0 \neq x^*_i$) or a false negative ($x_i \neq 0 = x^*_i$).

nodes.name: Successful reconstruction
nodes.statement: A certain value of the problem's parameters (such as number of individuals, number of lanes, read error etc.) is termed ``successful'' if at least $95\%$ of its instances (i.e. $475$ out of $500$) had {\it zero} reconstruction errors, namely {\it all} individual genotypes were reconstructed correctly.
differentia: at least $95\%$ of its instances (i.e. $475$ out of $500$) had {\it zero} reconstruction errors

nodes.name: Success criterion bounds the FDR
nodes.statement: In particular, this requirement guarantees that the False-Discovery-Rate of discovering rare-allele carriers will not exceed $0.05$.
conclusions: the False-Discovery-Rate of discovering rare-allele carriers will not exceed $0.05$

nodes.name: $N_{max}$
nodes.statement: Performance is then measured in terms of $N_{max}$, defined as the maximal number of individuals which allow for a ``successful'' reconstruction, for certain values of the problem's parameters.

nodes.name: Large groups with many lanes (f=0.1%)
nodes.statement: When the number of available lanes is large, we can successfully identify the carriers in groups of up to $9000$ or $20000$ individuals, for $k=500$ lanes, and $L=10$ or $L=1$, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:lanesAndNmax1Pro}(a,b).)
conclusions: we can successfully identify the carriers in groups of up to $9000$ or $20000$ individuals

nodes.name: Few lanes suffice for few carriers (f=0.1%)
nodes.statement: In case the number of available lanes is small we can still identify a single carrier out of $1000$ individuals with merely $k=20$ lanes, for $L=1$ and $L=10$. (inset in Fig.~\ref{fig:lanesAndNmax1Pro}(a,b).) With $k=30,40$ lanes, we can identify $2$ or $3$ carriers in a group of $2000$ or $3000$, for $L=1,10$, respectively.
conclusions: we can still identify a single carrier out of $1000$ individuals with merely $k=20$ lanes, for $L=1$ and $L=10$
With $k=30,40$ lanes, we can identify $2$ or $3$ carriers in a group of $2000$ or $3000$, for $L=1,10$, respectively

nodes.name: $N_{max}$ decreases with the number of loci $L$
nodes.statement: As is evident from the four panels of Fig.~\ref{fig:lanesAndNmax1Pro}, $N_{max}$ decreases as a function of $L$. For example, $500$ lanes are sufficient to deal with $20000$ individuals for $L=1$, but only with $1000$ individuals for $L=500$. This results from insufficient coverage which causes an increase in sampling noise.
conclusions: $N_{max}$ decreases as a function of $L$

nodes.name: $N_{max}$ grows almost linearly in $k$
nodes.statement: Increasing the number of lanes can overcome this under-sampling as the value of $N_{max}$ increases almost linearly with $k$ in most cases.
conclusions: the value of $N_{max}$ increases almost linearly with $k$ in most cases

nodes.name: Efficiency score
nodes.statement: In order to quantify the advantage of applying {\bf CS } we define an ``efficiency score'', presented in Fig.~\ref{fig:lanesAndNmax1ProES}, which is simply $N_{max}/k$, i.e., the number of individuals for which reconstruction can be performed using the {\bf CS } approach for a given number of lanes, divided by the number of individuals which can be treated using the naive one-individual-per-lane approach.
nodes.statement_short: Efficiency score $= N_{max}/k$, the gain over one individual per lane.

nodes.name: Efficiency score up to 70 (f=0.1%)
nodes.statement: When considering up to $L=100$ SNPs, the efficiency score is around or above $10$, and in some cases is as high as $70$.
conclusions: the efficiency score is around or above $10$, and in some cases is as high as $70$

nodes.name: Sharp success transition in coverage and lanes
nodes.statement: An improvement in performance may be achieved both by increasing the coverage and by increasing the number of lanes. The white line marks the $95\%$ accuracy threshold. The transition between ``successful'' and ``unsuccessful'' reconstruction is rather sharp. For low coverage, e.g., lower than $100$ reads per person, a very high number of lanes is needed in order to overcome sampling noise.
conclusions: The transition between ``successful'' and ``unsuccessful'' reconstruction is rather sharp.

nodes.name: Performance for f=1% and f=2%
nodes.statement: The resulting $N_{max}$ is lower than for the case of $f=0.1\%$, although still much higher than in the naive approach. Results for $L=1$ are similar to those of $L=10$, namely increasing the coverage does not improve performance significantly in this case. The differences between results for $f=1\%$ and $f=2\%$ are rather small. The ``efficiency score'' in this case is lower (see Fig.~\ref{fig:lanesAndNmax1Per2PerES}), and is around $5$, still offering a considerable saving compared to the naive approach.
conclusions: The resulting $N_{max}$ is lower than for the case of $f=0.1\%$, although still much higher than in the naive approach
is around $5$, still offering a considerable saving compared to the naive approach

nodes.name: Homozygous carriers handled by the same framework
nodes.statement: Our {\bf CS } framework deals with this scenario in exactly the same way as the other $AB$ cases, although the results are, as expected, slightly worse than that of $2\%$ heterozygous carriers.

nodes.name: Effect of sampling error
nodes.statement: Differences between the cases appear only when the number of SNPs is high, thus the number of reads per person $c$ is insufficient. In these cases $N_{max}$ is reduced by a factor of $2$ to $4$ with respect to an infinite coverage. When the number of SNPs is small, and coverage is high, we see no difference between the ``standard'' performance and the infinite read case.
conclusions: In these cases $N_{max}$ is reduced by a factor of $2$ to $4$ with respect to an infinite coverage

nodes.name: Effect of read errors
nodes.statement: In the absence of read errors $N_{max}$ may be twice as large as when $e_{r}=1\%$. Read errors take a significant effect on performance only when $L$ is large ($100$ or $500$), since when coverage is high read errors are compensated for (see Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt_noise}).)

nodes.name: Robustness to DP errors
nodes.statement: In all cases we have studied the results are quite robust to {DP } errors, thus noise introduced by realistic pooling protocols should be easily overcome by the {\bf CS } reconstruction.

nodes.name: Sparse ($\sqrt N$) sensing matrix
nodes.statement: Here we shortly present the possibility of modifying $M$ into a {\it sparse} sensing matrix, thus accommodating the requirement of having few individuals per pool.

nodes.name: Dense vs sparse pools
nodes.statement: For a small number of loci taken together ($L=1$ or $10$) the former dense Bernoulli(0.5) sensing matrix achieves higher $N_{max}$ values. However, when the number of loci is large ($L=100$ or $500$) and for large number of lanes, it is preferable to use sparse pools of size $\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: Optimal sparsity of the sensing matrix
nodes.statement: Further research is needed in order to determine the optimal sparsity of the sensing matrix for a given set of parameters.

nodes.name: Barcodes dramatically increase $N_{max}$
nodes.statement: Incorporating even a small number of barcodes into our {\bf CS } framework results in a dramatic increase in $N_{max}$.

nodes.name: Diminishing returns of many barcodes
nodes.statement: As long as the coverage is kept high, it is still beneficial to increase the number of barcodes, as it effectively increases linearly the number of lanes. At a certain point, when many different barcodes are present in a single lane, coverage drops and sampling error becomes significant, hence the advantage of adding more barcodes starts to diminish.

nodes.name: Highest rare-allele frequency for CS
nodes.statement: The highest frequency possible for {\bf CS } to perform well in this application was not determined, but one should expect a certain frequency above which it is no longer beneficial to apply {\bf CS } and the naive one-individual-per-lane approach is preferable.

nodes.name: CS beneficial up to about 5% frequency
nodes.statement: The simulations we have performed estimate this frequency to be over $5\%$ in most cases, thus taking effect only for the case of {\it common} alleles.

nodes.name: Joint optimization of pool design
nodes.statement: Therefore, one needs to optimize the pool design together with other parameters, e.g. number of loci and lanes considered. This issue remains for future study.

nodes.name: Unknown constant read error
nodes.statement: We assume that the read error $e_r$ is unknown to the researcher, but is constant across all lanes.
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error

nodes.name: Read-error convolution $\mathbf z * e_r$
nodes.statement: We replace $\textbf{z}$ in Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt}) by the convolution: \begin{equation} \textbf{z} * e_r \equiv \textbf{z} + e_r - 2 \textbf{z} e_r \end{equation}
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error

nodes.name: Convolution $\mathbf z*e_r$
nodes.statement: \textbf{z} * e_r \equiv \textbf{z} + e_r - 2 \textbf{z} e_r
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error

nodes.name: Auxiliary variable $x_{N+1}$
nodes.statement: We can approximate it by $x_{N+1} \equiv e_r - 2 \bar{z} e_r$, obtained from averaging the term $2 \textbf{z} e_r$ over all $\textbf{z}$ values (i.e. $\bar{z}$ is the mean value of the vector $\textbf{z}$).
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error

nodes.name: CS problem with learned read error
nodes.statement: We can now reformulate the {\bf CS } problem by adding one extra variable. Specifically, the unknown vector $\textbf{x}$ is replaced by $\textbf{x'} = (\textbf{x}, x_{N+1})$ and Eq.~(\ref{eq:CSopt}) is replaced by: \begin{equation} {\textbf{x'}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x'}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x'}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: ||\frac{1}{2} \hat{M'}\textbf{x'}-\frac{1}{r}\textbf{z'}||_2 \leq \epsilon \end{equation} where $M'$ is built from $M$ by adding a constant column to its right as its $N+1$'s column with all its values set to $-1$.
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error
nodes.statement_short: Augment x with $x_{N+1}$ and M with a constant $-1$ column, then solve the $\ell_1$ problem to learn $e_r$ jointly.

nodes.name: Augmented CS problem
nodes.statement: {\textbf{x'}}^* = \underset{\textbf{x'}}{argmin} ||\textbf{x'}||_1 \quad s.t. \: \: ||\frac{1}{2} \hat{M'}\textbf{x'}-\frac{1}{r}\textbf{z'}||_2 \leq \epsilon
nodes.section: A Coping with unknown read error
nodes.label: eq:cs_problem_L1_unknown_p_err
